\chapter{The Core Verbs}
\label{ch:mr-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use six everyday Marathi verbs, pick the present-tense ending that agrees with my subject's gender, end every sentence on the verb, and say that I know something the way Marathi says it — with the knower in the dative and \mr{आहे} closing the line.}

Say \mr{मला} \mr{माहीत} \mr{आहे} and \mr{मला} \mr{मराठी} \mr{येते} unprompted: the knower in the dative, the verb agreeing with its own subject rather than with the speaker, and \mr{आहे} closing the sentence — the whole chapter's machinery in two lines.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[asṇe]{\mr{असणे} (asṇe) — \textquotedblleft{}to be,\textquotedblright{} and the word your sentence ends on}

\label{lesson:MR-C07-asne}



\begin{quote}
You have already said it: \emph{mājhaṁ nāv … āhe}. Now meet the verb that form belongs to, and notice where Marathi insists on putting it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{असणे} and its present \mr{आहे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{असणे}} — \emph{asṇe} — \textbf{to be}
\end{quote}

The ending \textbf{-\mr{णे}} (\emph{-ṇe}) is the Marathi infinitive, the same ending as \emph{bolṇe} \textquotedblleft{}to speak.\textquotedblright{} Its present tense is short, irregular, and already yours: \textbf{\mr{आहे}} (\emph{āhe}) — \textquotedblleft{}am, is, are.\textquotedblright{}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{who} & \textbf{Marathi} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
\mr{मी} (I) & \textbf{\mr{आहे}} & \emph{āhe} \\
\mr{तू} (you, familiar) & \textbf{\mr{आहेस}} & \emph{āhes} \\
\mr{तुम्ही} (you, respectful) & \textbf{\mr{आहात}} & \emph{āhāt} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\mr{अ}} is the bare vowel \emph{a}; \textbf{\mr{स}} is \emph{sa}; \textbf{\mr{णे}} is the retroflex \textbf{\mr{ण}} \emph{ṇa} carrying the \emph{-e} stroke — \emph{a-sa-ṇe}. \textbf{\mr{आ}} is that first letter with an upright stroke added, the long \emph{ā}. \textbf{\mr{हे}} is \textbf{\mr{ह}} \emph{ha} with the same \emph{-e} stroke: \emph{ā-he}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
Sanskrit's word for \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} was \textbf{\mr{अस्ति}} \emph{ásti}, sitting on the stem \emph{as-}, and that stem goes back to the Indo-European root \textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}es-}. It surfaces almost everywhere the family reaches: Latin \emph{est}, Greek \emph{estí}, German \emph{ist}, and English \textbf{is}. \emph{Asṇe} is built straight on it.

\textbf{\mr{आहे}} itself is the contested piece. Some trace it to \emph{ásti} directly; others route it through a Middle Indo-Aryan verb \emph{acchai} \textquotedblleft{}stays, remains.\textquotedblright{} The family is not in doubt, the exact line of descent is — so treat it as an open question rather than a settled fact.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the sentence ends on \mr{आहे}}]
English slots \emph{is} into the middle of a sentence: \textquotedblleft{}My name \textbf{is} Sara.\textquotedblright{} Marathi holds it back to the very end:

\textbf{\mr{माझं} \mr{नाव} \mr{सारा} \mr{आहे}} — \emph{mājhaṁ nāv Sārā āhe} — piece by piece, \textquotedblleft{}my name Sara is.\textquotedblright{}

That is the rule for every Marathi verb, and \emph{āhe} is where it becomes unmissable. Whatever else the sentence carries, the verb closes it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}asṇe\textquotedblright{} — to be — then its present, \textquotedblleft{}āhe\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three persons — \textquotedblleft{}mī āhe … tū āhes … tumhī āhāt\textquotedblright{}
  \item your own name in Marathi order — \textquotedblleft{}mājhaṁ nāv … āhe\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the infinitive behind \emph{āhe}? (\textbf{\mr{असणे}}, \emph{asṇe}.) Where does a Marathi verb stand? (\textbf{Last} — the sentence closes on it.) Which everyday English word is \emph{ásti}'s own cousin? (\emph{\textbf{Is}}.) Next: a verb that changes shape according to who is speaking.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jāṇe]{\mr{जाणे} (jāṇe) — \textquotedblleft{}to go,\textquotedblright{} and a present tense that gives you away}

\label{lesson:MR-C07-jane}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}my name is …\textquotedblright{} once more, and hear where \emph{āhe} lands. Every verb from here obeys that same rule. This one adds a second rule English has no use for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{जाणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{जाणे}} — \emph{jāṇe} — \textbf{to go}
\end{quote}

Strip the infinitive ending \textbf{-\mr{णे}} and the stem is \textbf{\mr{जा}-} \emph{jā-}. On that stem Marathi builds the everyday present: \textbf{\mr{जातो}} (\emph{jāto}) and \textbf{\mr{जाते}} (\emph{jāte}).

Both mean \textquotedblleft{}I go.\textquotedblright{} Neither is more correct than the other. Which one you may say is decided by something the English sentence never mentions.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\mr{ज}} is \emph{ja}, and the upright stroke after it is the long \emph{ā} — together \textbf{\mr{जा}} \emph{jā}. \textbf{\mr{णे}} you met last lesson: retroflex \textbf{\mr{ण}} with the \emph{-e} stroke. Two syllables, \emph{jā-ṇe}, with the tongue curled back for that second one.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending declares who is speaking}]
English \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} hides the speaker completely — a man and a woman say the same two words. Marathi will not let you:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{speaking of} & \textbf{Marathi} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
a man, of himself & \mr{मी} \mr{जातो} & \emph{mī jāto} \\
a woman, of herself & \mr{मी} \mr{जाते} & \emph{mī jāte} \\
a man, \textquotedblleft{}he goes\textquotedblright{} & \mr{तो} \mr{जातो} & \emph{to jāto} \\
a woman, \textquotedblleft{}she goes\textquotedblright{} & \mr{ती} \mr{जाते} & \emph{tī jāte} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \textbf{-\mr{तो}} / \textbf{-\mr{ते}} swap is the whole mechanism, and it runs through every verb: \emph{bolto / bolte}, \emph{yeto / yete}. Hindi marks gender on its verbs too, but Marathi makes it unavoidable in the plainest sentence a beginner can build. From your first \textquotedblleft{}I go,\textquotedblright{} you are choosing.

Notice also what is missing: no separate word for \textquotedblleft{}am.\textquotedblright{} The ending carries the action, the person, and the gender at once.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}jāṇe\textquotedblright{} — to go — then the stem, \textquotedblleft{}jā-\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} in your own gender — \textquotedblleft{}mī jāto\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}mī jāte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}to jāto … tī jāte\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the stem inside \emph{jāṇe}? (\textbf{\mr{जा}-}, \emph{jā-}.) Which two endings split the present, and by what? (\textbf{-\mr{तो} / -\mr{ते}}, by the gender of the one the verb is about.) Can a Marathi speaker say \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} without revealing it? (\textbf{No} — the choice is forced.) Next: the same ancient root, pointed the other way.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yeṇe]{\mr{येणे} (yeṇe) — \textquotedblleft{}to come,\textquotedblright{} the other half of \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C07-yene}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} in your own gender: \emph{mī jāto} or \emph{mī jāte}. Hold that shape. The next verb is closer to it than it sounds.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{येणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{येणे}} — \emph{yeṇe} — \textbf{to come}
\end{quote}

Same infinitive ending, same machinery: stem \textbf{\mr{ये}-} \emph{ye-}, present \textbf{\mr{येतो}} (\emph{yeto}) and \textbf{\mr{येते}} (\emph{yete}), split by gender exactly as \emph{jāto / jāte} was.

You met \emph{yeto} in Chapter 4 as a farewell — Marathi takes its leave by saying \textquotedblleft{}I come,\textquotedblright{} promising the return rather than announcing the departure.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\mr{य}} is \emph{ya}, a soft English \emph{y} as in \emph{yes}. Add the \emph{-e} stroke above and you have \textbf{\mr{ये}} \emph{ye} — the same stroke you have been putting on \textbf{\mr{णे}} and on \textbf{\mr{हे}} in \emph{āhe}. Two syllables: \emph{ye-ṇe}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
Sanskrit had a verb of travelling, \textbf{yā-}, whose present was \textbf{\mr{याति}} \emph{yāti} \textquotedblleft{}goes, travels.\textquotedblright{} Middle Indo-Aryan turned that initial \emph{y-} into a \emph{j-}, giving Prakrit \emph{jāi} — and that is Marathi \textbf{\mr{जाणे}}.

Now put a prefix on it. Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{आ}-} \emph{ā-} means \textquotedblleft{}toward, hither,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\mr{आयाति}} \emph{āyāti} is \textquotedblleft{}travels toward here\textquotedblright{} — that is, \textbf{comes}. Worn down through the same centuries, \emph{āyāti} is Marathi \textbf{\mr{येणे}}.

So \emph{going} and \emph{coming} are not two verbs in this family. They are one verb of travelling, and the only difference is a prefix meaning \textquotedblleft{}this way.\textquotedblright{} English keeps a faint echo of the same trick in \emph{go} against \emph{in-coming}, but it needs two separate roots to do what Sanskrit did with one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}yeṇe\textquotedblright{} — to come — then the stem, \textquotedblleft{}ye-\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{} in your own gender — \textquotedblleft{}mī yeto\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}mī yete\textquotedblright{}
  \item the derivation — \textquotedblleft{}yāti … āyāti … yeṇe\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the stem of \emph{yeṇe}? (\textbf{\mr{ये}-}, \emph{ye-}.) Which Sanskrit root do \emph{jāṇe} and \emph{yeṇe} share? (\textbf{yā-}, to travel.) What single piece turns going into coming? (The prefix \textbf{\mr{आ}-} \emph{ā-}, \textquotedblleft{}toward here.\textquotedblright{}) Next: an infinitive that is also a noun, and the gender Hindi does not have.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khāṇe]{\mr{खाणे} (khāṇe) — \textquotedblleft{}to eat,\textquotedblright{} and Marathi's third gender}

\label{lesson:MR-C07-khane}



\begin{quote}
Two infinitives so far: \emph{jāṇe}, \emph{yeṇe}. Say them. This third one is ordinary as a verb and quietly remarkable as a noun.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{खाणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{खाणे}} — \emph{khāṇe} — \textbf{to eat}
\end{quote}

Stem \textbf{\mr{खा}-} \emph{khā-}, present \textbf{\mr{खातो}} (\emph{khāto}) and \textbf{\mr{खाते}} (\emph{khāte}) on the gendered pattern you already have.

Its root is Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{खादति}} \emph{khādati}, \textquotedblleft{}chews, eats\textquotedblright{} — a solidly Indo-Aryan word with no borrowing in its history. The \emph{-d-} wore away on the road to Marathi; the long \emph{ā} stayed.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\mr{ख}} is \emph{kha} — a \emph{k} with a genuine puff of breath after it, the sound in English \emph{kit} said hard, not the \emph{k} of \emph{skit}. Marathi treats that puff as a different letter, not an accent. Add the long-\emph{ā} stroke and the familiar \textbf{\mr{णे}}: \emph{khā-ṇe}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the infinitive is a neuter noun}]
\textbf{\mr{खाणे}} also simply means \textquotedblleft{}eating\textquotedblright{} — the thing, not the act of doing it. Every \emph{-\mr{णे}} infinitive works this way; \emph{\mr{खाणंपिणं}} (\emph{khāṇaṁ-piṇaṁ}), \textquotedblleft{}eating and drinking,\textquotedblright{} is how Marathi says food and drink.

And as a noun it carries a gender — \textbf{neuter}, the third one. Hindi has two genders, masculine and feminine. Marathi kept all three that Sanskrit had, so words agreeing with a noun come in three shapes:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{gender} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
masculine & \mr{चांगला} & \emph{chāṅglā} \\
feminine & \mr{चांगली} & \emph{chāṅglī} \\
neuter & \mr{चांगलं} & \emph{chāṅglaṁ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \textquotedblleft{}eating is good\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{\mr{खाणं} \mr{चांगलं} \mr{आहे}} — \emph{khāṇaṁ chāṅglaṁ āhe}, with the neuter ending twice over and the verb, as always, last.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}khāṇe\textquotedblright{} — to eat — then \textquotedblleft{}I eat\textquotedblright{} in your own gender
  \item the three shapes — \textquotedblleft{}chāṅglā … chāṅglī … chāṅglaṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eating is good\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}khāṇaṁ chāṅglaṁ āhe\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two things \textbf{\mr{खाणे}} means? (\textbf{To eat}, and \textbf{eating} as a noun.) How many genders does Marathi have, and how many does Hindi have? (\textbf{Three} against \textbf{two} — Marathi kept Sanskrit's neuter.) Which gender is an infinitive? (\textbf{Neuter}.) Next: a verb whose root you already own in a dozen English words.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pāhṇe]{\mr{पाहणे} (pāhṇe) — \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} a root you already own}

\label{lesson:MR-C07-pahne}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I eat\textquotedblright{} in your own gender — \emph{mī khāto} or \emph{mī khāte}. The next verb runs on the same endings, and on a root you have been using in English all your life without knowing it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{पाहणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पाहणे}} — \emph{pāhṇe} — \textbf{to see, to watch}
\end{quote}

Stem \textbf{\mr{पाह}-} \emph{pāh-}, present \textbf{\mr{पाहतो}} (\emph{pāhto}) and \textbf{\mr{पाहते}} (\emph{pāhte}). In everyday speech you will also hear \textbf{\mr{बघणे}} (\emph{baghṇe}) for the same job; \emph{pāhṇe} is the one whose history repays digging.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\mr{प}} is \emph{pa} without the puff of breath that \emph{kha} had. Add the upright stroke for long \emph{ā}: \textbf{\mr{पा}} \emph{pā}. Then \textbf{\mr{ह}} \emph{ha}, and the \textbf{\mr{णे}} you now know by heart. Three light syllables, \emph{pā-ha-ṇe}, usually spoken as two: \emph{pāh-ṇe}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
Sanskrit's verb for seeing was \textbf{\mr{पश्यति}} \emph{paśyati}, on the root \emph{paś-}, and Marathi's \emph{pāhṇe} descends from its prefixed form \textbf{\mr{प्रपश्यति}} \emph{prapaśyati}, \textquotedblleft{}looks out at.\textquotedblright{}

Now the payoff. That \emph{paś-} is the Indo-European root \textbf{*spek-}, \textquotedblleft{}to observe.\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit dropped the \emph{s-} and swapped the consonants around; Latin kept them in order as \emph{speciō}, \textquotedblleft{}I look.\textquotedblright{} From the Latin side English inherited an enormous family, every one of them a cousin of \emph{pāhṇe}:

\textbf{spect}acle, in\textbf{spect}, re\textbf{spect}, su\textbf{spect}, pro\textbf{spect}, \textbf{spec}ies, \textbf{spec}imen, \textbf{spec}ulate, tele\textbf{scope}, and — through Italian — \textbf{spy}.

So a Marathi speaker asking you to \emph{pāhṇe} something is asking you to \emph{inspect} it, in the most literal ancestral sense the word has.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pāhṇe\textquotedblright{} — to see — then \textquotedblleft{}I see\textquotedblright{} in your own gender
  \item the derivation — \textquotedblleft{}paśyati … prapaśyati … pāhṇe\textquotedblright{}
  \item four English cousins — \textquotedblleft{}spectacle, inspect, species, spy\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the stem of \emph{pāhṇe}? (\textbf{\mr{पाह}-}, \emph{pāh-}.) Which Sanskrit verb is it from? (\textbf{\mr{पश्यति}} \emph{paśyati}, in its prefixed form \emph{prapaśyati}.) Name three English words from the same ancient root. (\emph{Spectacle, inspect, species, spy} — any three.) Next: a verb Marathi mostly refuses to use, and what it says instead.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[māhīt asṇe]{\mr{माहीत} \mr{असणे} (māhīt asṇe) — \textquotedblleft{}to know,\textquotedblright{} which Marathi says sideways}

\label{lesson:MR-C07-mahit-asne}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{} in your own gender — \emph{jāto} or \emph{jāte}, \emph{yeto} or \emph{yete}. Five verbs obeyed that pattern. This one refuses.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{माहीत} \mr{असणे} and \mr{जाणणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{माहीत} \mr{असणे}} — \emph{māhīt asṇe} — \textbf{to know} (everyday)
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{जाणणे}} — \emph{jāṇṇe} — \textbf{to know} (formal, literary)
\end{quote}

Marathi has an inherited verb for knowing and barely uses it. Everyday speech says \emph{māhīt asṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to be known,\textquotedblright{} built on \emph{asṇe}.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\mr{म}} is \emph{ma}; with the long-\emph{ā} stroke, \textbf{\mr{मा}}. \textbf{\mr{ही}} is \textbf{\mr{ह}} \emph{ha} with the long \emph{-ī} stroke, which leans forward ahead of its letter. \textbf{\mr{त}} is \emph{ta}: \emph{mā-hī-t}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: knowledge comes to you, you do not do it}]
\textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{माहीत} \mr{आहे}} — \emph{malā māhīt āhe} — \textquotedblleft{}I know.\textquotedblright{}

Word by word: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to me} known \textbf{is}.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Malā} is \textquotedblleft{}to me,\textquotedblright{} and the knower sits there, not in the subject slot. Nobody acts; a fact is simply in your possession, and \emph{āhe} closes the line.

The same frame carries a language: \textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{मराठी} \mr{येते}} — \emph{malā marāṭhī yete} — \textquotedblleft{}I know Marathi,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}to me Marathi comes.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Yete} is feminine because the subject is \textbf{\mr{मराठी}}, a feminine noun — not the speaker; a man says it too. The verb agrees with its subject, as always. Here the subject is not you.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{माहीत}} is a \textbf{loan}: through Persian from Arabic \emph{māhiyat}, \textquotedblleft{}the particulars\textquotedblright{} — one of the administrative words the Deccan sultanates left in Marathi.

\textbf{\mr{जाणणे}} is pure inheritance: Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{जानाति}} \emph{jānāti}, root \emph{jñā-}, from Indo-European \textbf{*gnō-} — the root of English \textbf{know}, Latin \emph{nōscere} (\emph{notice}, \emph{recognize}) and Greek \emph{gnōsis} (\emph{diagnosis}). Marathi kept the cousin and gave the daily work to the loan.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}malā māhīt āhe\textquotedblright{} — then literally, \textquotedblleft{}to me known is\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I know Marathi\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}malā marāṭhī yete\textquotedblright{}
  \item the inherited verb and its English cousin — \textquotedblleft{}jāṇṇe … know\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does Marathi put the knower? (\textbf{In the dative} — \emph{malā}, \textquotedblleft{}to me.\textquotedblright{}) Which verb finishes \emph{malā māhīt āhe}, and where? (\textbf{\mr{आहे}}, \textbf{last}.) Why \emph{yete} in \emph{malā marāṭhī yete}? (The subject is \textbf{\mr{मराठी}}, feminine — agreeing with it, not the speaker.) Which know-verb was borrowed? (\textbf{\mr{माहीत}}, through Persian.)
\end{tcolorbox}
